blocks.text: The space around the Earth in which its gravitational force acts on a body is called the gravitational field. When an object is moved in the gravitational field, work is done by the gravitational force: if the displacement is in the direction of the gravitational force the work is positive, and if the displacement is against the gravitational force the work is negative. The gravitational force has an interesting property: when an object is moved from one place to another, the work done by the gravitational force does not depend on the choice of path.

Consider an object of mass m displaced with constant speed from point A to point B along various paths in the presence of a gravitational force (Fig. 4.9); the gravitational force equals the weight mg of the object. The work done by the gravitational force along path 1 (ADB) can be split into two parts: the work along AD is zero, because the weight mg is perpendicular to this path; the work along DB is -mgh, because the direction of mg is opposite to that of the displacement (theta = 180 degrees). Hence the work done in displacing the body from A to B through path 1 is W_ADB = 0 + (-mgh) = -mgh. Along path 2 (ACB) the work along AC is also -mgh and the work along CB is zero, so W_ACB = -mgh + 0 = -mgh. Now consider path 3, a curved one: imagine it broken into a series of horizontal and vertical steps (Fig. 4.10). No work is done along the horizontal steps, because mg is perpendicular to the displacement there; work is done by gravity only along the vertical displacements. During the segment AB, mg is not negative, it is positive, but all the delta y elements are negative, so the products of mg and delta y for all the elements are again negative: W_AB = -mg (delta y1 + delta y2 + delta y3 + ... + delta yn), and as delta y1 + delta y2 + ... + delta yn = h, W_AB = -mgh. The net work along path AB is still -mgh. A smooth path may be replaced by a series of infinitesimal x and y displacements; work is done only during the y displacements.

blocks.title: Conservative force
blocks.text: Work done by the gravitational force is independent of the path followed. Can you prove that the work done along a closed path such as ACBA or ADBA (Fig. 4.9) by the gravitational force is zero? If the work done by a force in moving an object between two points is independent of the path followed, or the work done in a closed path is zero, the force is called a conservative force. The gravitational force is conservative; other examples are the electrostatic force and the elastic spring force.

blocks.title: Non-conservative force
blocks.text: Not all forces are conservative. A force is non-conservative if the work done by it in moving an object between two points, or in a closed path, depends on the path of motion.

The kinetic frictional force is non-conservative. When an object slides over a surface, the kinetic frictional force acts opposite to the motion and does negative work equal in magnitude to the frictional force multiplied by the length of the path; thus a greater amount of work is done over a longer path between any two points, so the work depends on the choice of path. Moreover, the total work done by a non-conservative force in a closed path is not zero. Other examples of non-conservative forces are air resistance, tension in a string, the normal force and the propulsion force of a rocket.
